papers.title: Isoflurane anesthesia CNS recovery state: ultra-slow oscillations and cellular-stress-responsive gene expression
papers.abstract: General anesthesia and NREM sleep share slow-wave EEG features, yet whether anesthesia substitutes for physiological sleep remains unclear. We compared recovery from 4h of isoflurane anesthesia (IA) with time-matched sleep and sleep deprivation (SD) in male C57BL/6J mice using continuous EEG/EMG recordings and frontal cortex RNA sequencing. IA recovery produced transient, rebound arousal, reduced early NREM and REM sleep, and, fragmented subsequent NREM bouts, and persistant, ultra-slow EEG-oscillations that normalized within two weeks. Whereas, SD induced consolidated rebound sleep and slow wave activity. Transcriptomic profiling at ZT6 showed that IA and SD induced largely distinct cortical gene-expression programs. IA preferentially enriched integrated stress response and unfolded protein response genes, whereas SD showed a comparatively orthogonal, growth-permissive, mTOR-associated profile. Although IA-induced gene-expression suggests cellular stress, corticosterone measurements argued against systemic stress as the primary driver. These findings indicate that isoflurane recovery is neurophysiologically and molecularly distinct from restorative sleep.

papers.title: Firing Without Wiring: How REM-like Sleep Reactivation Rebalances Excitation and Inhibition to Orthogonalize Memories
papers.abstract: The role of Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep in memory consolidation remains poorly understood. Several influential ideas propose that REM sleep serves to eliminate crosstalk between memories, thereby orthogonalizing representations of similar ones; however, mechanistic confirmation remains sparse. Here we used recurrent neural networks trained with Equilibrium Propagation (EP), a biologically plausible training algorithm, to investigate the role of REM-like sleep in memory consolidation. We found that REM-like sleep reduces memory interference by decorrelating task-specific neuronal populations, isolating individual memory traces. During sleep, reactivation was dominated by the population encoding the most recent memory. Net excitatory input onto this population decreased, most strongly that from older-memory populations, which allowed inputs of older memories to drive their own neurons again. Spreading the same total synaptic change evenly across all target populations abolished this recovery. We call this mechanism reactivation-targeted pruning: plasticity is confined to one population, whose neurons lose inputs that are silent when they fire. The mechanism held under Dale's law, and depression of excitatory synapses alone, without any inhibitory plasticity, was sufficient. These findings suggest mechanistic principles underlying REM sleep's role in memory consolidation and highlight the potential for integrating human-like learning behaviors into artificial neural networks.

This mechanism held under Dale's law and required only excitatory synaptic depression, without inhibitory plasticity.

papers.title: Zona incerta circuits in cognition and the regulation of sleep and wakefulness: potential relevance to Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by progressive cognitive decline and prominent disturbances in sleep and wakefulness, reflecting dysfunction across distributed neural networks. The zona incerta (ZI) is a highly heterogeneous subthalamic structure whose organization is defined by spatial location, molecular identity, neurochemical phenotype, and circuit connectivity. Recent studies demonstrate that distinct ZI cell populations and projections contribute to memory processing, novelty seeking, cortical plasticity, sleep promotion, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, transitions to wakefulness, and sleep homeostasis. Together, these findings suggest that the ZI is better viewed as a state-dependent subcortical regulatory platform than as a unitary cognitive or sleep center. Emerging pathological evidence further raises the possibility that the ZI may be relevant to neurodegeneration. Amyloid-β deposition has been reported in the ZI of 5xFAD transgenic mice, while experimental tau propagation, human tauopathies other than AD, and studies of other neurodegenerative disorders indicate potential cellular and circuit vulnerability. However, direct evidence from human AD remains lacking, and no study has established a causal pathway from AD pathology to selective ZI dysfunction and subsequent cognitive or sleep impairment. We therefore propose two testable models in which the ZI contributes to AD phenotypes either as a shared circuit node or through parallel, selectively vulnerable functional modules.

papers.title: Layer 1 NDNF interneurons form distinct subpopulations with opposite activation patterns during sleep in freely behaving mice
papers.abstract: Non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep facilitates memory consolidation by transferring information from the hippocampus to the neocortex. This transfer is thought to occur primarily when hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SWRs) and thalamocortical spindles are synchronized. However, the mechanisms underlying this synchronization remain unknown. In this study, we investigated the role of cortical layer 1 NDNF-expressing (L1 NDNF) interneurons in gating information transfer during SWR-spindle synchronization in NREM sleep. Using simultaneous cell-specific calcium imaging with a head-mounted microscope and local field potential recordings in freely moving mice, we compared the activity of L1 NDNF and L2/3 neurons across vigilance states and during NREM-specific oscillations. Our findings reveal that L1 NDNF neurons form three distinct populations, assembling into cell networks tuned to specific sleep stages. REM active L1 NDNF and L2/3 neurons exhibit opposite activation patterns during spindles. While L2/3 cells are mostly inactive during SWR, NREM, and REM active L1 NDNF cells inhibit the network upon SWR onset depending on their coupling with spindles. L1 NDNF neurons mediate slow inhibition primarily via GABAB receptors. Systemic application of a GABAB receptor antagonist resulted in decreased neuronal coupling of pyramidal cells but did not change the inhibitory responses during SWRs. Overall, these findings highlight the potential role of L1 NDNF neuron-mediated inhibition in the response to synchronized sleep oscillations, with potential implications for memory consolidation.

papers.title: Behavioral, Transcriptomic, and Neuroinflammatory Effects of Sleep Deprivation: Insights From Separate Acute and Chronic Experimental Paradigms.
papers.abstract: Depression is a global health burden associated with sleep disruption and inflammation. While acute sleep deprivation (ASD) can alleviate depressive symptoms, chronic sleep deprivation (CSD) is a risk factor for mood disorders. However, the contrasting mechanisms underlying these opposing outcomes remain poorly understood. We integrated behavioral profiling, multi-region transcriptomics, and multiplex cytokine analysis to separately characterize the effects of ASD in a pain-depression comorbidity model and CSD in normal mice. Adult male C57BL/6J mice (n = 6 per group) were subjected to either a single 6-h total sleep deprivation (ASD) or 6-h daily sleep deprivation for 14 consecutive days (CSD). Behavioral testing included the tail suspension test (TST), open field test (OFT), elevated plus maze (EPM), and sucrose preference test (SPT). Following the interventions, five brain regions-prefrontal cortex (PFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), agranular insular cortex (AI), parietal cortex (PAR), and retrosplenial cortex (RSP)-were dissected. Cytokine levels were quantified using a multiplex panel targeting 15 analytes. Behavioral tests demonstrated that ASD alleviated despair-like behaviors induced by spared nerve injury surgery, whereas CSD resulted in anxiety- and despair-like behaviors. The prefrontal cortex (PFC) exhibited prominent transcriptomic responses to both ASD and CSD, with a substantial number of differentially expressed mRNAs. Transcriptome sequencing confirmed stable differential expression of mRNAs across multiple brain regions. Notable genes linked to depression, including Plin4 and Sult1a1, emerged as potential targets for further research. Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of differentially expressed mRNAs in the PFC indicated that IL-6 and TNF were primarily associated with these changes following ASD. Additionally, inflammatory factors such as BAFF, CHI3L1, IL-4, IL-6R alpha, IL-6, IL-10, TNFRSF1B, IL-12 p70, TWEAK, and osteopontin significantly decreased in the ASD group but increased in the CSD group. This study elucidates that ASD is associated with alleviation of despair-like behaviors and concurrent suppression of multiple inflammatory factors; however, the causal relationship between these observations requires further experimental validation. These findings open new research avenues for identifying potential depression treatment targets. Future research should explore the functional implications of these transcriptomic changes and their relevance for developing novel antidepressant strategies. These findings open new research avenues for identifying potential depression treatment targets. papers.title: EEG Pathology Detection via Clinical Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.abstract: Deep learning models for electroencephalography (EEG) pathology detection achieve competitive accuracy but offer limited interpretability. In this paper, we introduce concept bottleneck models (CBMs) for EEG pathology detection which use clinical EEG biomarkers computed analytically from the signal as a bottleneck to be used for prediction. Those concepts include band power, spectral ratios, alpha peak frequency and amplitude, hemispheric asymmetry and phase locking values. With the backbone based on shallow convolutional neural network (CNN), we compare a black box baseline with two variants of CBMs. The hybrid variant is a classifier receives a residual projection of the backbone features. The pure variant is a CBM where the classifier receives only the predicted concepts. Models are evaluated on abnormality detection and dementia classification followed by concept prediction quality and leakage analysis. Both CBMs approach the baseline on TUAB (82.7-82.9% vs 83.6%) and are 2-5 percentage points lower on CAUEEG (57.9-60.5% vs 62.7%). The pure CBM exhibits concept fidelity concern where the predicted concepts deviate from their ground truth values. Replacing them with their true values causes severe cost on accuracy by 26 and 22 points on TUAB and CAUEEG. The concept fidelity concern is mitigated by increasing the weight of the concept loss to match the ground truth concepts. the mitigation comes with small accuracy cost on TUAB but a relatively larger cost on CAUEEG. The code of the experiments and full logs are available at https://www.github.com/mhmdrdwn/cbm.

papers.title: Phasic pupil responses to melanopsin- and cone-directed stimulation remain stable across circadian time
papers.abstract: Human pupil responses vary with time of day, but whether this reflects circadian modulation of specific photoreceptor pathways is unclear. Twelve healthy adults completed repeated pupillometry during a 40-hour ultra-short sleep-wake protocol that limited sustained wakefulness; data from eight met the quality-control criteria and were analysed. This design was intended to limit progressive accumulation of homeostatic sleep pressure across sampled circadian phase. During wake episodes, 0.4-Hz silent-substitution stimuli targeted broadband flux, melanopsin, luminance, L-M cone-opponent, or S-cone pathways. Salivary melatonin provided participant-specific period estimates. We separated slow tonic constriction from phasic pupil tracking and compared hierarchical circadian cosinor models with constant-level models. Constant-level models were favoured for phasic amplitude in all five conditions (log10 BF10 = -3.36 to -1.10). They were also favoured for tonic minimum in four conditions; L-M favoured the circadian model (log10 BF10 = 0.67), but the evidence was imprecise. Under the tested contrast, adaptation, and frequency, these data do not support circadian modulation of phasic photoreceptor-directed pupil tracking. Other metrics and smaller or non-sinusoidal effects remain possible.

papers.title: Sleep-state transition instability with recurrent multisystem activation: A case-based phenotypic framework.
papers.abstract: The wake-to-sleep transition is a physiologically vulnerable period during which benign and pathologic motor phenomena may emerge. Current sleep nosology recognizes isolated hypnic jerks, propriospinal myoclonus at sleep onset, sleep-related rhythmic movement disorder, and other minor sleep-related motor activities, but these entities may not fully explain patients with persistent, repetitive motor activation recurring across successive attempts to fall asleep. We describe eight representative cases characterized by recurrent motor events centered on sleep onset or early sleep-state transitions, associated sensory and autonomic symptoms, clinically meaningful sleep fragmentation, and absence of a more satisfactory alternative diagnosis. On the basis of these observations, we introduce sleep-state transition instability with recurrent multisystem activation (SSTI-RMA) as a provisional, hypothesis-generating phenotypic construct rather than an established diagnostic entity. The recurring clinical pattern comprises recurrent motor activation during wake-to-sleep or early sleep transitions together with variable sensory, autonomic, cardiovascular, respiratory, or other non-motor manifestations, repetition or clustering of events, difficulty initiating or stabilizing sleep, clinically significant distress or impairment, and absence of a more satisfactory alternative explanation. We conceptualize the SSTI-RMA phenotype as a possible disorder of sleep-state instability rather than as an isolated motor phenomenon, potentially involving impaired coordination among neural, autonomic, and vascular processes during sleep entry. No validated polysomnographic signature, frequency threshold, biomarker, or prevalence estimate is currently available, and the relationship of this phenotype to severe or recurrent sleep starts remains unresolved. SSTI-RMA should therefore be regarded as a descriptive research framework intended to facilitate standardized phenotyping and prospective studies capable of determining whether it represents a distinct entity, part of a continuum of established sleep-onset phenomena, or a heterogeneous phenotype with multiple causes.

papers.title: Sleep underestimation and subjective sleep appraisal: Limited value of routine polysomnographic and electroencephalographic features.
papers.abstract: Whether routine polysomnographic (PSG) and electroencephalographic (EEG) features distinguish patients who underestimate sleep remains unclear. We examined associations of clinical, subjective, PSG, and EEG features with sleep underestimation and tested whether EEG features added discrimination beyond a parsimonious three-predictor baseline model. We analysed 225 adults undergoing clinically indicated in-laboratory PSG in this single-centre retrospective cross-sectional study. The misperception index ([objective - subjective total sleep time]/objective total sleep time) was dichotomised at the cohort median (0.148) and analysed continuously. Group differences across 717 variables underwent Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Out-of-fold (OOF) discrimination was compared between a three-predictor baseline model (sleep quality, Epworth Sleepiness Scale score, and age) and an EEG-enhanced model; continuous-index analyses were exploratory. Fifty-six participants (24.9%) overestimated sleep. Objective total sleep time did not differ between groups, whereas self-rated sleep quality did (q = 0.002). None of 600 EEG features survived FDR correction (smallest q = 0.064). At the median threshold, OOF areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) were 0.6786 (baseline) and 0.6564 (EEG-enhanced; ΔAUC = -0.0221; paired DeLong P = 0.4483). Across 50 repeated partitions, median ΔAUC was -0.0261 for EEG features and +0.0096 for four macrostructural PSG variables. Obstructive sleep apnoea prevalence did not differ significantly between groups. Self-rated sleep quality was more consistently associated with sleep underestimation than routine PSG and EEG features. EEG features did not demonstrate incremental OOF discrimination beyond the baseline model. Subjective sleep appraisal should be assessed alongside PSG; underlying mechanisms require prospective investigation.

papers.title: Sleep Stage Classification Across Heterogeneous EEG/EOG Channels with Multi-channel Differential Transformer.
papers.abstract: Classification of sleep stages is essential for assessing sleep quality and diagnosing sleep disorders. However, manual inspection of EEG characteristics for each stage is time-consuming and prone to human error. Although machine learning and deep learning methods have been actively developed, they continue to face challenges arising from the non-stationarity and variability of electroencephalography (EEG) and electrooculography (EOG) signals across diverse clinical configurations, often resulting in poor generalization. In this work, we propose SleepDIFFormer, a multi-channel differential transformer framework for heterogeneous EEG-EOG representation learning. SleepDIFFormer is trained across multiple sleep staging datasets, each treated as a source domain, with the goal of generalizing to unseen target domains. Specifically, it employs a Multi-channel Differential Transformer Architecture (MDTA) designed to process raw EEG and EOG signals while incorporating cross-domain alignment. Our approach mitigates spatial and temporal attention noise and learns a domain-invariant EEG-EOG representation through feature distribution alignment across datasets, thereby enhancing generalization to new domains. Empirically, we evaluated SleepDIFFormer on five diverse sleep staging datasets under domain generalization settings and benchmarked it against existing approaches, achieving superior performance. Furthermore, comprehensive ablation analyses and interpretation of the differential attention weights demonstrated their relevance to learning discriminative sleep EEG representations. These findings support the development of more generalizable approaches to automated sleep-stage classification. Our source code and checkpoint are made publicly available at https://github.com/Ben1001409/SleepDIFFormer.

papers.title: REM Atonia Index Cutoffs for REM Sleep Without Atonia: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis of Adult Diagnostic Performance.
papers.abstract: To synthesize evidence on REM Atonia Index (RAI) thresholds and reference values, quantify adult diagnostic performance for REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and distinguish diagnostic cutoffs from physiological reference limits and pediatric values. Methods: We conducted a focused systematic review of studies using automated RAI, rescreening studies from a previous review and updating PubMed/MEDLINE through July 27, 2026. Adult diagnostic accuracy was synthesized with a bivariate binomial-normal random-effects model. Continuous RAI differences were pooled as raw mean differences. Normative adult and pediatric evidence was synthesized separately because these represented different estimands. The review was retrospectively registered in OSF Registries on August 20, 2026 (https://osf.io/v3kqa). Thirty unique studies were included. Eight adult studies contributed to the diagnostic-accuracy meta-analysis; thresholds ranged from 0.80 to 0.90. Pooled sensitivity was 0.850 (95% CI, 0.766-0.908) and specificity 0.895 (95% CI, 0.814-0.944). Eight studies contributed continuous data; RAI was lower in RBD by a pooled mean difference of -0.263 (95% CI, -0.335 to -0.190). Only two methodologically non-equivalent adult studies provided physiological reference limits, 0.85 and 0.91, precluding pooling. Pediatric evidence supported age-conditioned interpretation. Adult chin-EMG RAI shows good overall discrimination of established RBD, but current evidence does not support a universal numerical boundary for REM sleep without atonia. Evidence defining physiological reference limits is substantially less developed than diagnostic evidence, and normal RAI varies with age. RAI should therefore be reported continuously, with thresholds interpreted according to their intended diagnostic or physiological purpose.

papers.title: Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome: Unloading the Respiratory System with Expiratory Pressure.
papers.abstract: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) is traditionally interpreted through the lens of coexistent obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), yet the mechanisms by which continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) improves daytime hypercapnia without providing ventilatory support remain incompletely explained. This Perspective proposes that abdominal obesity-induced depletion of expiratory reserve volume (ERV) and functional residual capacity (FRC), with consequent reduction in end-expiratory lung volume (EELV), may represent upstream mechanical abnormalities linking OSA, increased work of breathing, sleep hypoventilation, and daytime hypercapnia. Reduced EELV worsens pharyngeal collapsibility by decreasing caudal traction, while simultaneously shifting tidal volume toward a mechanically inefficient portion of the respiratory system curve, characterized by impaired compliance, and increased elastic, resistive respiratory work and possibly threshold loading. Within this framework, OHS emerges when respiratory burden (the mechanical load on the pulmonary apparatus due to excess weight) exceeds ventilatory reserve (an ensemble of respiratory drive and its modifiers such as sleep-state control, leptin signaling, and genetic factors). CPAP and expiratory PAP may provide, in addition to upper-airway splinting, a mechanical unloading by raising EELV, improving respiratory mechanics, and reducing the pressure cost of ventilation. In this context, weight loss represents the ultimate structural unloading therapy, whereas pressure support may be required when unloading alone is insufficient to restore adequate ventilation. Future studies should measure ERV, FRC/EELV, respiratory effort, and mechanics to better phenotype OHS, and understand whether optimizing expiratory pressure before adding ventilatory support actually improves ventilation.

papers.title: Nonlinear Feature Modeling Using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Electroencephalography for Depression Classification: Deep Learning Study.
papers.abstract: Depression is a common mental disorder that seriously affects mental health and quality of life. Traditional depression diagnosis mainly relies on clinical interviews and subjective assessments, which may lead to variability in diagnostic outcomes. Electroencephalogram (EEG)-based computer-aided diagnosis has emerged as a promising, objective approach for depression recognition. However, effectively modeling the complex nonlinear characteristics of EEG signals remains a major challenge for existing deep learning methods. This study aimed to investigate the applicability of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) for EEG-based depression recognition and to evaluate the effectiveness of KAN-based nonlinear modeling frameworks on frequency-domain EEG features. KAN was introduced into EEG-based depression recognition to enhance nonlinear feature representation of brain electrical signals. Two representative KAN-based convolutional architectures, ConvKAN and its efficiency-optimized variant ConvKAN Efficient, were systematically investigated for EEG classification tasks. These architectures incorporated KANLinear layers together with dynamic grid updating, enhanced weight initialization, and regularization strategies to improve nonlinear modeling capability while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive experiments were conducted on the EDRA dataset, and the proposed framework was compared with conventional convolutional neural network-based methods and traditional machine learning approaches. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score metrics. Experimental results demonstrated that the KAN-based frameworks achieved superior EEG classification performance compared with conventional convolutional neural network-based methods and traditional machine learning approaches. Among the evaluated models, ConvKAN Efficient achieved the best overall performance, with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score all exceeding 94% on the EDRA dataset. The results indicate that KAN-based architectures can effectively capture the complex nonlinear characteristics of EEG signals while preserving high computational efficiency. This study systematically demonstrates the applicability of KAN-based nonlinear modeling frameworks to EEG-based depression recognition. The proposed framework provides a scalable and effective approach for EEG signal analysis and offers valuable technical support for both theoretical research and clinical applications in computer-aided depression recognition.

papers.title: Single-Lead EEG-based virtual reality motion sickness detection using interpretable feature selection.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a key method for detecting virtual reality motion sickness (VRMS), but multi-lead recordings and high-dimensional features increase processing complexity, device cost, and user burden. This study proposes a SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based single-lead modeling and feature-screening framework to reduce the number of EEG leads and feature dimensions for lightweight VRMS detection. Six classical deep-learning EEG decoding models were used to assess the contribution of each lead via SHAP values and identify the optimal single lead. Handcrafted features were then extracted and selected using a correlation-SHAP strategy, and XGBoost was adopted for final classification. FT11 showed competitive and relatively consistent performance across the evaluated models and was selected as the target lead after integrating SHAP-based lead importance, single-lead classification performance, frequency-band differences, and physiological relevance. Under the window-level tenfold cross-validation protocol used in this study, the proposed model achieved an accuracy of 87.53% ± 0.73% using seven selected features, which was 9.55 percentage points lower than the full-lead full-feature model and 0.69 percentage points lower than the single-lead full-feature model. These findings demonstrate an interpretable framework for identifying a compact single-lead and feature configuration for VRMS-related EEG discrimination. An additional post hoc LOSO test of the globally selected configuration showed limited performance on held-out participants. Because the lead, classifier, and feature configuration had been selected globally before LOSO testing, these results should not be interpreted as a fully independent estimate of cross-subject generalization.

papers.title: Astrocyte molecular rhythm disruption in nucleus accumbens promotes increased binge-like drinking in mice.
papers.abstract: Alcohol misuse is a leading cause of preventable death worldwide. Chronic alcohol is associated with disrupted circadian rhythms, yet molecular mechanisms linking circadian rhythm dysregulation and alcohol consumption are poorly understood. Current FDA-approved treatments for alcohol use disorder (AUD) do not target molecular rhythms or sleep-wake cycles. Mammalian circadian rhythms are regulated by transcription-translation feedback loops that regulate expression of 'clock genes' (e.g., Arntl encoding for BMAL1). Both human and rodent studies demonstrate associations between clock gene variants and changes in reward-seeking behavior. Evidence suggests astrocytes, non-neuronal brain cells with cell-autonomous rhythms, may regulate both circadian rhythms and reward. In the nucleus accumbens (NAc), a region responsible for modulating alcohol- and reward-related behavior, over 43% of the astrocyte transcriptome is expressed rhythmically. However, no studies to date have investigated roles of NAc astrocyte rhythmicity in regulating alcohol drinking. We used AAV8-Gfap-Cre to functionally ablate molecular rhythms in NAc astrocytes of BMAL1 floxed mice. Two-bottle choice (2BC), drinking-in-the-light (DIL), and drinking-in-the-dark (DID) assessed alcohol drinking. Behavioral assays included locomotor response to novelty, sucrose preference, and social interaction. Disrupting molecular clock function in NAc astrocytes increased binge-like drinking during both DIL and DID paradigms ( d = 1.44), but not with any other drinking paradigm or behavior. This study carves out a unique role for astrocytes in controlling the temporal organization of reward circuitry and susceptibility to binge-drinking. Future studies will investigate clock-controlled astrocyte mechanisms, such as glutamate uptake and ATP release, that may underlie binge-like drinking behavior.

papers.title: Circadian rhythms and sleep disturbances: a conceptual perspective with implications for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
papers.abstract: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is a genetic disorder characterized by cyst formation, kidney enlargement, and extrarenal complications. While the role of genetic mutations in PKD1, PKD2, and other minor genes is well established, the influence of circadian rhythms and sleep disturbances on disease progression remains underexplored. The circadian timing system, coordinated by the central clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus and synchronized with peripheral clocks in the kidneys, regulates key physiological processes, including glomerular filtration rate (GFR), sodium handling, blood pressure, and hormone secretion. In ADPKD, circadian disruption driven by intrinsic molecular alterations and exacerbated by sleep disorders contributes to sympathetic nervous system activation, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) dysregulation, and elevated vasopressin levels, all of which accelerate cyst growth and hypertension. Mechanistic links also involve the activation of the mTOR pathway, impaired fatty acid oxidation, and altered gut microbiota composition. These disturbances impair kidney function and increase the risk of cardiovascular disease. Chronotherapy and targeted sleep hygiene interventions offer promising adjunctive strategies for mitigating circadian misalignment in ADPKD. Timed administration of antihypertensives, diuretics, and disease-modifying agents, such as tolvaptan, along with melatonin supplementation, structured light exposure, and optimized physical activity patterns, may enhance therapeutic efficacy and improve quality of life (QoL). Future research should prioritize longitudinal and interventional studies incorporating circadian biomarkers to evaluate the impact of aligning therapeutic interventions with biological rhythms on kidney and cardiovascular outcomes in ADPKD.

papers.title: Spectral power and functional connectivity of resting EEG in people exposed to armed conflict and controls
papers.abstract: Exposure to armed conflict can leave persistent effects on mental health, yet its neurophysiological correlates remain poorly characterized, particularly in populations exposed to prolonged violence outside narrowly defined post traumatic stress disorder samples. Here we examined resting state electroencephalographic activity in 122 Colombian adults, including 74 participants exposed to armed conflict and 48 controls. Eyes closed EEG was analysed for 240 seconds per participant. We quantified absolute and relative spectral power across delta, theta, alpha and beta bands and regional functional connectivity using weighted phase lag index in theta, alpha and beta. Group comparisons were adjusted for age, education, sex and assessment year, with correction across 78 EEG contrasts. Median occipital and global alpha power was lower in exposed participants, although adjusted estimates were close to the null and confidence intervals were broad. Temporal theta relative power was lower in exposed participants at nominal significance, but this association did not survive Holm correction. No spectral power or regional connectivity contrast remained significant after multiple testing correction. Exploratory associations between EEG measures and MoCA performance were modest in participants with confirmed scores. These findings provide a systematic characterization of resting EEG after exposure to armed conflict in a population shaped by prolonged violence and displacement. They also indicate that large or widespread alterations in resting spectral power and connectivity were not detectable with the current sample and analytical framework, while defining candidate signals and methodological priorities for larger studies of conflict related brain health.

papers.title: A Humanized Mouse Model of DRPLA Recapitulates Epilepsy and Demonstrates Antisense Oligonucleotide-Mediated Disease Modification
papers.abstract: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is an ultra-rare progressive myoclonus epilepsy caused by a glutamine-coding CAG repeat expansion in atrophin-1 (ATN1). Mutant ATN1 (mATN1) expression results in symptoms that inversely correlate to CAG-expansion size: young-onset cases have the most CAG repeats and developmental delay, high-frequency treatment-resistant seizures, and early mortality. We sought to characterize the seizure susceptibility of a fully humanized ATN1 mouse expressing human mATN1 with 112 CAG repeats to then assess therapeutic antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) intervention on seizure-related outcomes. Atn1Q112/+ or wild-type (WT) mice were treated with investigational ASO targeting human, CAG-expanded, ATN1 or saline (P2 and then again at 4 weeks-old) before acute seizure testing, ataxia profiling, and chronic in vivo video-EEG recording for spontaneous seizures up to 8 weeks-old. Saline-treated Atn1Q112/+ mice were more seizure prone with early death. However, ASO administration to Atn1Q112/+ mice normalized seizure threshold, decreased ataxia, and protected against early death. Atn1Q112/+ mice exhibited spontaneous behavioral seizures recorded over 2 weeks, which were absent in ASO-treated Atn1Q112/+ and WT mice, with a specific mATN1 expression-driven decrease in delta and theta EEG frequencies. Atn1Q112/+ mice are highly seizure prone, validating this model for DRPLA epilepsy. ATN1 represents a novel epilepsy-related risk factor for therapeutic investigation.

papers.title: De-escalating Therapy in Obstructive Sleep Apnoea After Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonist-Induced Weight Loss: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Incretin-based therapies now achieve weight reduction of a magnitude previously attainable only through bariatric surgery and have demonstrated substantial reductions in the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) in adults with obesity-related obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). Sleep services are consequently managing growing numbers of patients who undergo rapid, substantial weight loss while established on positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy, and who ask whether that therapy can be stopped. No guideline addresses this question. This narrative review synthesises three literatures that have developed largely in isolation: the relationship between weight change and OSA severity, the efficacy data for glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and dual incretin agonists in OSA, and the experimental PAP withdrawal literature. Across randomised trials and meta-analyses, there is consistent agreement that incretin therapy reduces AHI, body weight and blood pressure, with effect magnitude varying by agent, dose and baseline adiposity. There is, however, material disagreement on three questions directly relevant to de-escalation: whether the effect is wholly weight-mediated, whether AHI reduction translates into reduction in cardiovascular risk, and what proportion of patients achieve genuine disease remission as opposed to severity reduction. Approximately half of participants in the largest trial did not reach a severity threshold at which PAP would ordinarily be considered unnecessary, and withdrawal studies demonstrate recurrence of obstructive events and adverse haemodynamic change within days of stopping therapy. This review proposes a structured, reversible and documented framework for reassessment rather than ad hoc discontinuation and identifies the evidence gaps that must be closed before de-escalation can be considered evidence-based practice.

papers.title: Composite sleep patterns and the allergy-related composite outcome among American and Chinese older adults: exploration of depressive symptoms as a potential mediator.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances and depressive symptoms commonly co-occur in older adults, but their associations with heterogeneous allergy-related outcomes and the role of depressive symptoms remain unclear. We analyzed 1,562 participants aged ≥60 years from NHANES 2005-2006. A composite sleep pattern combined sleep duration, trouble sleeping, and diagnosed sleep disorders. The allergy-related composite outcome comprised elevated total immunoglobulin E and seven questionnaire-assessed disease or symptom outcomes. Survey-weighted logistic regression evaluated associations. Depressive symptoms were assessed with a modified 8-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8), and statistical mediation examined indirect associations through its continuous score. We also conducted a complementary longitudinal analysis in 6,146 Chinese older adults from CHARLS. Poor versus healthy sleep was associated with higher odds of the allergy-related composite outcome (OR 2.100; 95% CI 1.328-3.322), wheeze (OR 2.148; 95% CI 1.296-3.559), and sneeze (OR 1.636; 95% CI 1.135-2.357). The estimated indirect association through depressive symptoms represented 22.5% of the total association. In CHARLS, impaired sleep quality was associated with incident asthma (OR 1.689; 95% CI 1.254-2.275), and the corresponding indirect association through depressive symptoms represented 28.3% of the total association. Poor sleep was associated with heterogeneous allergy-related outcomes among US older adults, while CHARLS provided complementary longitudinal evidence for incident asthma. Depressive symptoms statistically accounted for part of the observed sleep-allergy association.

papers.title: The impact of creatine on brain functions.
papers.abstract: As an endogenous compound essential for energy homeostasis, creatine holds a fundamental role in the bioenergetics of the brain, an organ with high metabolic requirements. This review provides a synthesis of current knowledge on the impact of creatine on the functions of the central nervous system (CNS). The brain, which is capable of de novo creatine synthesis, demonstrates an increase in its internal concentrations following supplementation; however, this effect is less significant than in muscle tissue and is constrained by the blood-brain barrier, among other factors. The development of effective CNS-targeted dosing strategies remains a subject of ongoing research. An overview of the literature suggests that creatine supplementation may beneficially influence cognitive performance, particularly under conditions of elevated metabolic demand like stress or sleep deprivation, with the potential to enhance memory and mitigate fatigue. Nonetheless, findings from the cited research are inconsistent due to methodological heterogeneity and a common failure to directly measure brain creatine levels. Reports on creatine's antidepressant properties are particularly encouraging, with preclinical and initial clinical studies pointing to its potential utility (e.g., via the mTORC1 pathway) in augmenting mood disorder treatments. Moreover, the authors examine the use of creatine in chronic fatigue syndrome, where evidence supports improvements in physical performance and reductions in pain intensity, although its effect on generalized fatigue remains ambiguous.

papers.title: Prebiotics in sport and exercise: current evidence, practical applications, and methodological considerations.
papers.abstract: Prebiotics are selectively utilized by the host microbiota and can confer health and/or performance benefits, in part through increasing the abundance of beneficial gut microorganisms and their metabolites. While several studies have shown promising initial findings, high-quality scientific evidence examining the effects of prebiotics on athlete performance, health and wellbeing remains limited. This narrative review summarizes the current available evidence on prebiotic intake in athletic populations, including effects on gastrointestinal structure and function, immune responses, recovery, sleep, wellness, mood and exercise performance. In areas where there is limited evidence in athletic cohorts, but a physiological rationale for a benefit, findings from sedentary and/or clinical populations are evaluated, and the potential relevance of these findings to athletes are discussed. Finally, considerations for practitioners around the use of prebiotics with athletes are provided, and recommendations for designing future prebiotic-based research are explored. Despite the limited existing literature around prebiotic use in athletes, there are several studies that indicate their potential to improve gut barrier integrity and reduce the incidence/severity of gastrointestinal symptoms. Data also indicates that prebiotics can increase salivary Immunoglobulin A secretion rate and reduce the duration and/or severity of upper respiratory symptoms in trained individuals. Other areas with emerging evidence that warrant further investigation in athletic populations include prebiotics' ability to support exercise adaptation and recovery, promote sleep improvements and enhance mood and cognitive function. The interpretation of current studies is limited by the lack of gut microbiome and metabolome measures and the absence of robust performance measures following a period of prebiotic supplementation. Well-controlled, adequately powered studies incorporating these outcomes are needed to determine the contexts in which prebiotic intake can meaningfully improve health and performance metrics, and to elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of any beneficial effects. Prebiotic intake represents a promising intervention to attenuate exercise-induced disturbances to the intestinal epithelium, reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, and lower the duration/severity of upper respiratory symptoms in athletes. Future studies should prioritize high-quality performance assessments, alongside comprehensive microbiome and metabolome profiling, to elucidate mechanistic effects. Areas with limited current evidence such as recovery, sleep, mood, cognitive function, bone health and nutrient absorption in athlete cohorts should also be further explored.

papers.title: Responses to unannounced rule changes in adults with developmental disabilities: A community-based pilot study with consumer-grade EEG
papers.abstract: Unannounced changes in rules or environments often precede challenging behavior and limit community participation for adults with developmental disabilities, yet their responses to change have rarely been quantified directly. We recruited adults with developmental disabilities, including those with intellectual disability, at a community day-service center. We administered a probabilistic reversal learning task and recorded resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) via a 14-channel wireless EEG system. Among the 12 adults who performed the task, total errors were comparable across participants (range 31-57), whereas a switch bias index, contrasting perseverative errors (persisting with the previously correct option) with regressive errors (failing to maintain the newly correct option), ranged from -0.96 to +0.91. In the 9 participants included in resting-state EEG analyses, a flatter aperiodic spectrum over the frontal cluster (preregistered, but selected as the focus post hoc) was associated with fewer switches after negative feedback ({rho} = .80) and more perseverative errors ({rho} = -.72). The preregistered parieto-occipital cluster showed the same direction ({rho} = .69, 95% confidence interval [-.11, .97], n = 8), which was opposite to the preregistered prediction. Frontal alpha peak amplitude was associated with accuracy ({rho} = .77), and the between-run reliability of resting-state measures was .82-.99. These findings provide preliminary evidence that EEG recorded in community settings can capture individual differences in how people respond to change. Field measurement that includes people with intellectual disability may help extend the evidence base for the Sustainable Development Goals of good health and well-being (SDG 3) and reduced inequalities (SDG 10).

papers.title: The qualitative exploration of work productivity among chronic rhinitis patients.
papers.abstract: Chronic rhinitis is a global public health concern affecting sleep, cognitive function, mood, quality of life, and work performance. It contributes to socioeconomic costs through decreased productivity, including absenteeism and presenteeism. This study explores the impact of chronic rhinitis on work productivity and employee performance to inform better management strategies. A literature review and semi-structured interviews were conducted with 19 chronic rhinitis patients from Hospital Canselor Tuanku Muhriz and Hospital Ampang. Data saturation was reached, and thematic analysis was performed using Atlas.ti. Eight themes were identified: absence during working hours, work limitations, disruption of social interactions, reduced work efficiency, emotional disturbances, weaknesses in compliance with work procedures, sleepiness at work, and negative perceptions from colleagues. Chronic rhinitis significantly affects work productivity, leading to absenteeism, reduced efficiency, and workplace stigma. These findings highlight the need for targeted management strategies to improve work performance and reduce the negative impact of chronic rhinitis on affected individuals.

papers.title: [The association between circadian rhythm disruption-related behaviors and myopia in children and adolescents].
papers.abstract: Child and adolescent myopia has become a critical global public health concern, with its prevalence steadily rising worldwide. Shifts in circadian behaviors, including irregular sleep schedules and increased nighttime exposure to artificial light, have contributed to widespread circadian rhythm disruptions manifested as sleep disorders, social jetlag, and excessive nighttime blue light exposure. Accumulating evidence suggests that circadian rhythm-disrupting behaviors are closely linked to the onset and progression of myopia in children and adolescents, although the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This paper systematically reviews the associations between circadian rhythm-disrupting behaviors and pediatric and adolescent myopia, as well as the potential pathogenic mechanisms involved. It further summarizes existing myopia intervention strategies targeting circadian behavioral abnormalities. By optimizing circadian behavioral patterns, this review aims to provide novel insights and evidence for the precise prevention and control of childhood and adolescent myopia.

papers.title: A novel age-based physiological definition of adherence to pediatric long-term non-invasive ventilation: an exploratory study.
papers.abstract: The indications for pediatric long-term non-invasive ventilation (LT-NIV) have expanded. However, a standardized definition of pediatric adherence is lacking. To propose a novel physiological definition of adherence to pediatric LT-NIV and compare it with the two commonly used adult-derived definitions. Retrospective cross-sectional study including all eligible children aged 0.15-18 years enrolled in the LT-NIV follow-up program at Hospital Garrahan, Argentina. Clinical data were obtained from medical records and adherence from device memory downloads. The proposed definition classified patients as "adherent" when LT-NIV use reached ≥ 70% of the minimum age-specific recommended sleep duration (American Academy of Sleep Medicine consensus) on ≥ 70% of nights, replacing a fixed threshold with one tailored to each child´s sleep needs. This was compared to the current(≥ 4 h/night on ≥ 70% of nights) and classic (≥ 4 h/night on ≥ 50% of nights) adult-derived definitions. Eighty patients were included (median age 9.01years, IQR 5.96-14.09). The most frequent diagnoses were neuromuscular (31%) and genetic disorders (15%). LT-NIV was initiated electively in 91%, 75% reported sleep-disordered breathing symptoms, polysomnography was abnormal in 95.2%. Adherence rates were 66.25% (novel definition); 83.75% (classic definition) and 78.75% (current definition), p = 0.0005 and p = 0.0039 respectively. Poorer adherence was associated with younger age, developmental delay, absence of symptoms, earlier ventilation initiation and lower pressure settings. Our results highlight an overestimation of adherence when adult definitions are used. This first study explores a novel pediatric adherence definition for LT-NIV. Our research calls for action to discuss new international pediatric adherence thresholds.

papers.title: Gut microbiome composition and cardiometabolic risk among healthcare workers: findings from the EXPONIT study.
papers.abstract: The gut microbiome plays an important role in metabolic regulation and has been linked to cardiometabolic disorders. Circadian-related factors (night shift work, sleep quality, chronotype) may influence gut microbiome characteristics and cardiometabolic health. We aimed to investigate the associations between gut microbiome diversity and composition and cardiometabolic outcomes, and evaluate whether these associations differ by work schedule, sleep quality, and chronotype. Fecal samples were taken on a working day, and gut microbiota composition was assessed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Anthropometric measures (body mass index,waist-to-hip ratio, systolic and diastolic blood pressure) and blood samples (metabolic biomarkers), were obtained during study visits. Associations between microbial composition and cardiometabolic outcomes were examined using robust linear and logistic regression models. Potential interactions with shift work status, sleep quality, and chronotype were also explored. Overall, alpha diversity was not significantly associated with cardiometabolic markers. However, overall gut microbiome composition (beta diversity) was associated with excess body weight (PERMANOVA p = 0.01, R2 = 0.7%). In addition, specific genera were associated with anthropometric markers: greater relative abundance of Lachnospiraceae-unclassified-genus-008 was associated with a higher body mass index; and increased relative abundance of Escherichia/Shigella and lower relative abundance of Alistipes were associated with higher waist-to-hip ratio. No associations were found between beta diversity or taxonomic composition and metabolic biomarkers. Specific gut microbial profiles may be associated with cardiometabolic markers, particularly obesity-related traits. Future longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the directionality and underlying mechanisms of these associations.

papers.title: A Reproducible Safety Assessment Model for Concurrent Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation with Implanted Intracranial Electroencephalography Electrodes.
papers.abstract: Concurrent transcranial magnetic stimulation and intracranial EEG (TMS-sEEG) offers a powerful approach for interrogating human brain circuits with high spatiotemporal resolution. However, standardized safety testing procedures for TMS in the presence of implanted electrodes are lacking. To establish and validate a reproducible methodological framework for assessing TMS safety with sEEG hardware, addressing potential risks of electrode displacement, heating, and secondary current induction. A conductive agarose phantom implanted with clinical-grade platinum sEEG electrodes was exposed to single-pulse TMS (0.4 Hz), repetitive TMS (1-50 Hz), and intermittent theta burst stimulation. Electrode displacement was quantified via high-speed video and motion tracking. Temperature changes were measured with fiber-optic thermal probes positioned at stimulated electrode contacts. Induced voltages were recorded using an oscilloscope and intracranial EEG hardware, and secondary current and charge density were calculated from oscilloscope outputs and impedance measurements. sEEG lead displacement remained micrometer-scale across stimulation conditions, with a maximum transient displacement of 10.99 μm and a maximum 1-s mean displacement from the pre-TMS position of 16.27 μm. Temperature changes remained well within the 2°C safety threshold across all tested conditions; in the primary temperature series, the maximum observed increase was 0.073°C. Induced voltages and charge densities remained below established safety limits, exhibiting consistent exponential decay with increasing distance from the coil. All stimulation conditions, including those exceeding typical clinical ranges, remained well within safety margins. Under the tested conditions in a controlled phantom environment, TMS exposure produced micrometer-scale transient and longer-timescale displacement, temperature changes within established safety thresholds, and charge densities within established safety thresholds. This validated methodological pipeline provides a standardized framework for future safety experiments involving TMS and implanted devices and supports continued development of TMS-sEEG as a tool for studying human brain circuitry and neuromodulation.

papers.title: Differential Cerebral Perfusion Patterns Across Migraine Phenotypes: An Exploratory ASL MRI Study.
papers.abstract: This study aims to characterize cerebral blood flow (CBF) alterations across migraine phenotypes and determine whether perfusion measures provide additional information for phenotype differentiation. The final cohort comprised 143 patients with migraine and 49 healthy controls who underwent three-dimensional pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling (ASL) MRI. Voxel-wise analyses of normalized CBF (nCBF) were performed to identify phenotype-related perfusion alterations. Sensitivity analyses repeated the voxel-wise comparisons with phenotype-appropriate clinical covariates. Exploratory correlation analyses examined associations between regional perfusion and clinical characteristics. Logistic regression was further used to assess whether perfusion measures provided additional information for differentiating migraine with aura (MA) from migraine without aura (MO). Compared with healthy controls, migraine patients with depressive symptoms showed reduced nCBF in a right hippocampus-parahippocampal cluster (Cluster 1) in the primary voxel-wise analysis; however, this finding did not survive additional adjustment for sleep quality. Lower Cluster 1 nCBF was associated with greater headache frequency. Compared with MO, patients with MA showed increased nCBF in a right cerebellar-occipitotemporal cluster peaking in the right cerebellar Crus I (Cluster 2), and this difference remained significant after additional adjustment for sleep quality, medication-overuse headache status, and preventive medication exposure. Within the MA group, higher Cluster 2 nCBF was associated with greater headache intensity. In exploratory logistic regression analysis, the combined clinical-imaging model showed a higher apparent area under the curve (AUC) than the clinical model alone. Clinically relevant migraine phenotypes showed distinct patterns of regional cerebral perfusion. These findings highlight the importance of considering clinical heterogeneity in migraine neuroimaging and suggest that ASL-derived perfusion measures may provide complementary biological information for phenotype characterization, particularly with respect to aura status.

papers.title: Enhancement of gut-microbiome-based classification of prodromal Parkinson's Disease cases by hyperparameter tuning, integration of multimodal data, and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's Disease (PD) is often preceded by a prodromal phase marked by non-motor symptoms such as REM Sleep Behaviour Disorder (RBD), gastrointestinal dysfunction, and olfactory impairment. Mounting evidence implicates gut microbiota in the early pathophysiology of PD. In this study, we aimed to enhance the classification of prodromal PD using gut microbiota profiles, with a focus on model performance and biomarker identification. Publicly available gut microbiome datasets of individuals with RBD and healthy controls were analyzed. Following batch correction and genus-level filtering, we identified six taxa significantly depleted in both RBD and PD groups, all belonging to short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing genera. Hyperparameter tuning on the testing set achieved an AUC of 0.889. When combining microbial and clinical features, the model achieved a peak mean AUC of 0.917. Feature selection identified 11 top-ranked features, yielding an AUC of 0.849. Using only the six differentially abundant SCFA-producing taxa, the model retained a strong predictive capacity with a mean AUC of 0.853. These results demonstrate the utility of gut microbiota, particularly SCFA-producing taxa, in the early identification of prodromal PD. Integration with select clinical features further improves model performance, supporting their potential role in early diagnostic frameworks.

papers.title: Effects of an Esketamine-Containing Induction Regimen on Postoperative Sleep, Analgesia, and Postpartum Depression in Parturients with Sleep Disorders Undergoing Cesarean Section Under General Anesthesia: A Double-Blind Randomized Trial.
papers.abstract: Preoperative sleep disturbances in parturients undergoing cesarean section correlate with exacerbated postoperative pain and an elevated risk of postpartum depression. Although esketamine demonstrates analgesic and antidepressant benefits in the general cesarean population, its combined effects on sleep, analgesia, and mood remain poorly characterized in patients with pre-existing sleep impairment. This study investigated the efficacy of an esketamine‑containing induction regimen on postoperative sleep quality, analgesia, and early depressive symptoms in parturients with PSQI‑defined preoperative sleep disorders scheduled for elective cesarean section under general anesthesia. We conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving 90 parturients scheduled for elective cesarean section under general anesthesia. Participants were randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to receive either an esketamine-containing induction regimen (esketamine 0.25 mg/kg plus propofol 1.0 mg/kg; n=45) or a standard induction regimen (saline plus propofol 2.0 mg/kg; n=45). All 90 participants were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (missing data imputed), and 84 (41 vs 43) were included in the complete-case sensitivity analysis. The primary outcome was sleep quality on postoperative day (POD) 1, assessed using an 11-point sleep Numerical Rating Scale (NRS; 0=best, 10=worst; 24-hour recall). Secondary outcomes included sleep NRS scores on POD 3 and POD 42, and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) on POD 42 (exploratory); Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain scores at 2, 12, 24, and 48 hours, and rescue analgesic consumption over 72 hours; and Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) scores on POD 3 and POD 42 (≥13 indicating a positive result). The esketamine regimen significantly improved the primary outcome (sleep NRS on POD 1; mean difference [MD] = 3.0, 95% CI: 2.0 to 4.0; P < 0.001). Exploratory secondary outcomes showed early pain benefits and reduced rescue analgesia (risk ratio [RR] = 3.33, 95% CI: 0.98 to 11.32; absolute risk difference = 15.5%, 95% CI: 0.7% to 30.21%), but these differences were small with wide intervals. Continuous EPDS scores were lower on POD 3 (P = 0.004), while the exploratory binary analysis (EPDS ≥ 13) was not significant (RR = 1.22, 95% CI: 0.56 to 2.66; P = 0.613). No serious adverse events occurred; however, the trial was not powered for safety outcomes. An esketamine-containing induction regimen was associated with improved early sleep quality on POD 1 in parturients with preoperative sleep disorders undergoing cesarean delivery under general anesthesia. However, because the trial was not powered for secondary outcomes or safety, and the differing propofol doses prevent isolation of esketamine's specific effect, these secondary findings are exploratory. Further adequately powered trials are required to confirm these results and evaluate safety. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2300078490.

papers.title: Effect of a Subanesthetic Dose of Esketamine on Postoperative Sleep Disturbance After Oocyte Retrieval Under Intravenous Anesthesia: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) is a common complication after oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. This study aimed to evaluate whether a subanesthetic dose of esketamine reduces the incidence of PSD. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial included 196 women undergoing oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. Participants were randomly assigned to the esketamine or control group. During anesthesia induction, the esketamine group received an intravenous bolus of esketamine 0.2 mg/kg, whereas the control group received an equivalent volume of normal saline. The primary analysis was conducted according to the intention-to-treat principle, with missing outcome data handled using multiple imputation; 189 participants (95 in the control group and 94 in the esketamine group) were included in the per-protocol sensitivity analysis. The primary outcome was the incidence of PSD on postoperative day (POD) 3, defined using a composite criterion of an Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS) score ≥6 or a numerical rating scale (NRS) score ≥6. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of PSD on POD 1, postoperative pain scores, postoperative anxiety and depression scores, and patient satisfaction with the anesthetic technique. In the intention-to-treat analysis with multiple imputation, the estimated incidence of PSD on POD 3 was lower in the esketamine group than in the control group (13.06% vs 24.90%; risk difference, -11.84 percentage points [95% CI, -22.98 to -0.69]; relative risk [RR], 0.52 [95% CI, 0.28-0.99]; P = 0.047). The per-protocol (PP) sensitivity analysis yielded similar results (12.8% vs 24.2%; RR, 0.53 [95% CI, 0.28-0.99]; P = 0.043). PSD on POD 1 did not differ between the groups. No between-group differences in postoperative anxiety or depression scores were noted. Postoperative pain scores at 30 minutes were significantly lower in the esketamine group (P < 0.001). Dreaming was more frequent in the esketamine group (21.4% vs 11.2%; P = 0.048), and the time to full alertness (12 [10-14] vs 11 [9-13] minutes; P = 0.002) and postanesthesia care unit (PACU) stay (34 [30-37] vs 31 [29-34] minutes; P = 0.005) were modestly longer. A single subanesthetic dose of esketamine was associated with a lower incidence of short-term PSD on POD 3 in women undergoing oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. Larger multicenter studies are warranted to confirm these findings. China Clinical Trial Registry Identifier: ChiCTR2500105998.

papers.title: Acute Psychosis and Dissociative Syndrome Following Binge Recreational Nitrous Oxide Use: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Recreational nitrous oxide (N2O) inhalation is increasingly prevalent among young adults, but acute psychiatric presentations following short-term binge exposure remain poorly characterized. We report a case of a female in her early 20s with no prior history of psychotic illness who developed an acute psychotic and dissociative syndrome over three days at an outdoor music festival. Her presentation followed heavy recreational N2O and 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) exposure combined with sleep deprivation. On admission, she exhibited profound disorientation, inability to recognize close family members, polymorphic delusions, passivity phenomena, and auditory and olfactory hallucinations, requiring involuntary psychiatric hospitalization. Diagnostic workup revealed normal brain and cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and a normal electroencephalogram (EEG) without epileptiform activity or slowing. Serum homocysteine was moderately elevated (25.2 µmol/L) alongside a low-normal vitamin B12 concentration (270 pg/mL), consistent with N2O-induced functional cobalamin deficiency; both markers normalized following parenteral vitamin B12 and oral folic acid supplementation. During inpatient stay, treatment with risperidone was followed by progressive neutropenia, which fully resolved after cross-titration to aripiprazole. She gradually regained full insight, was discharged on day 12, and remained free of psychotic symptoms at her three-week outpatient review. This case suggests that short-term binge N2O exposure, together with MDMA and sleep deprivation, may contribute to severe neuropsychiatric presentations without chronic use; it illustrates the value of measuring homocysteine rather than relying solely on serum B12 levels; and highlights potential hematological adverse effects during antipsychotic initiation.

papers.title: Efficacy and Safety of Integrated Chinese and Western Medicine for Depression With Anxiety and Somatic Symptoms: A Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveSomatic symptoms are often linked with depression and anxiety, making diagnosis difficult and limiting treatment effectiveness. Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western medicine has been studied as a complementary approach; however, its efficacy and safety have not been systematically evaluated. This review and meta-analysis examined the effectiveness and safety of integrated Traditional Chinese and Western medicine in patients diagnosed with depression with or without comorbid anxiety and somatic symptoms.MethodsThis systematic review and meta-analysis followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. English-language studies published from 2014 to 2026 were searched in PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus. Randomized controlled trials comparing integrated therapy with control interventions were included. The primary outcome was depression severity assessed by HAMD scores. Secondary outcomes included anxiety symptoms, somatic symptoms, and adverse events. A random-effects model was used, and heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic.ResultsEleven studies met review criteria. Integrated therapy significantly reduced depression severity compared with the standard Western medicine control condition (MD = -3.95, 95% CI: -4.71 to -3.19; I2 = 59%). Anxiety symptoms were also significantly reduced (MD = -3.95, 95% CI: -4.65 to -3.26; I2 = 50%). Somatic symptoms, including sleep disturbances and pain-related outcomes, improved but were assessed descriptively because of reporting variability. Adverse events were lower or similar in combined treatment groups, indicating a favorable safety profile. Funnel plot analysis suggested minimal publication bias.ConclusionIntegrated Traditional Chinese and Western medicine was associated with greater improvements in depression and anxiety symptoms than the included control interventions, which comprised Western medicine alone, placebo/sham interventions, or usual care, while showing generally good tolerability. However, given the methodological limitations, heterogeneity of comparator conditions, and low certainty of the available evidence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.

papers.title: Interplay of action-based prediction and top-down attention: EEG evidence for joint modulation of late perceptual processing.
papers.abstract: Voluntary action shapes our perception through sensory predictions of its consequences. These predictions are thought to inhibit perceptual processing of predicted outcomes, leading to sensory attenuation. However, some studies have reported findings that contrast with this effect, suggesting that the influence of predictions may reflect, or interact with, attentional processes. Here, we investigated the interplay of action-based prediction and top-down attention on early and late perceptual processing, with prediction and attention referring to the likelihood of a sensory event and its behavioral relevance, respectively. Electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded while participants viewed two sequential gratings. The orientation of the first was either predicted and self-generated or unpredicted and externally generated. Participants judged the tilt direction of the second grating relative to the first but responded only when the grating appeared in a task-relevant color. EEG analyses revealed no modulation of early visual potentials (N1a), but modulations at later processing stages. Specifically, the P3b exhibited reduced amplitude for predicted compared to unpredicted stimuli, but only when they were task-relevant, whereas task-relevance enhanced the P3b only for unpredicted stimuli. Interestingly, multivariate pattern analysis showed significant temporal clusters for decoding the grating's orientation exclusively for predicted and task-relevant stimuli, although decoding performance did not significantly differ between conditions. Furthermore, predicted and task-relevant stimuli elicited faster behavioral responses, with prediction-related P3b latency differences correlating with reaction-time differences. Overall, converging findings from the P3b, multivariate, time-frequency and behavioral analyses provide suggestive evidence that top-down attention and action-based prediction may jointly facilitate late perceptual and decision-related processing.

papers.title: Cannabidiol (CBD) for Pain: A Narrative Review of Evidence to Date.
papers.abstract: Cannabidiol (CBD), the principal non-intoxicating phytocannabinoid of Cannabis sativa, is widely marketed and self-administered for pain relief, yet its regulatory status as an analgesic remains unapproved. This review synthesizes preclinical mechanistic data, human pharmacokinetic data, and clinical trial evidence across major pain conditions in order to summarize the current evidence for, or against, efficacy and safety for pain. A synthesis of published information was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, PubMed Central, Cochrane Library, ScienceDirect, and other databases, integrating findings from systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and pharmacology reviews on CBD (independent of combination products where possible) and pain of any etiology. Preclinical and mechanistic data support plausible physical analgesic pathways for CBD, including receptor modulation, indirect enhancement of endocannabinoid tone via fatty-acid-binding-protein (FABP) inhibition, and anti-inflammatory effects. However, translation to clinical benefit has been inconsistent. In the largest meta-analysis of cannabinoids for pain, cannabinoids reduced chronic pain and improved sleep quality, but effect sizes fell below predefined minimally important clinical differences, and cannabinoids showed no benefit for acute or cancer pain, while increasing non-serious adverse events. CBD randomized trials in knee osteoarthritis, fibromyalgia, and acute low back pain have consistently failed to separate from placebo, whereas smaller/lower-quality trials and observational surveys report subjective benefit. Safety data increasingly point to dose-dependent hepatotoxicity risk. Despite strong biological plausibility and considerable consumer use, current high-quality evidence does not support CBD monotherapy as an effective analgesic across most pain conditions studied to date. Safety monitoring, particularly of liver enzymes at higher doses, is warranted.

papers.title: Ayurveda in Integrative Oncology: Aligning Traditional Principles with Conventional Cancer Care.
papers.abstract: Patients challenged with cancer diagnosis and treatments often seek solutions beyond conventional therapies to improve their quality of life and immunity and to manage symptoms, concerns, coping, and daily functioning. Ayurveda, a traditional medical system originating in India, has generated growing interest within integrative oncology; however, limited clarity and evidence exist regarding its appropriate application and integration across the oncology care continuum. This paper explores the evolving landscape of integrative oncology, focusing on the incorporation of Ayurveda into global cancer care. With emphasis on evidence-based practices, we discuss the similarities and distinctions between Ayurvedic and integrative oncology approaches including nutrition, exercise, mind body practices, sleep, and use of herbal supplements. We aim to stimulate further dialogue and multidisciplinary collaboration between oncology healthcare providers and Ayurveda clinicians. Developing a patient-centered, evidence-informed, integrative model of care that incorporates Ayurvedic approaches has the potential to enhance the quality of life for patients along the cancer trajectory. This discussion may stimulate further research and medical education with the goal of incorporating supported Ayurvedic approaches into mainstream cancer care.

papers.title: Early Postoperative Psychological Resilience Patterns and Associated Factors in Patients with Knee Stiffness Undergoing Arthroscopic Release Surgery: A Latent Class Growth Model Study.
papers.abstract: Knee stiffness substantially impairs mobility and quality of life. Although arthroscopic release can improve joint function, little is known about early postoperative changes in psychological resilience among these patients. This study aimed to identify heterogeneous early postoperative psychological resilience patterns in patients with knee stiffness undergoing arthroscopic release surgery and to explore factors associated with pattern membership. A prospective observational study was conducted among patients undergoing arthroscopic release for knee stiffness. Psychological resilience was assessed using the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale at four time points: admission before surgery, 3 days after surgery, 2 weeks after surgery, and 1 month after surgery. Latent class growth modeling was used to identify early postoperative resilience pattern groups. Univariate analyses and multinomial logistic regression were conducted to explore factors associated with pattern membership. Multicollinearity among candidate predictors was assessed before multivariable modeling. A total of 240 patients completed all four assessments. The LCGM identified three early postoperative psychological resilience pattern groups: the Low Resilience Declining Group (17.1%), the Moderate Resilience Stable Group (68.8%), and the High Resilience Increasing Group (14.2%). Multinomial logistic regression using standardized continuous psychosocial predictors showed that, compared with the High Resilience Increasing Group, patients in the Low Resilience Declining Group had lower perceived social support and poorer sleep quality. Compared with the High Resilience Increasing Group, patients in the Moderate Resilience Stable Group were more likely to have a primary-school education or below, lower perceived social support, and lower ERRI scores. Psychological resilience showed heterogeneous patterns during the early postoperative period after arthroscopic release for knee stiffness. The findings may help identify patients who are psychologically vulnerable during early recovery, but should be interpreted as exploratory because of the single-center design, short follow-up duration, and limited subgroup sizes. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up and orthopedic outcome measures are needed to validate these early postoperative patterns and clarify their clinical significance. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s43465-026-01903-1.

papers.title: Comparative analysis of pain experience and quality of life in patients with oral lichen planus and burning mouth syndrome.
papers.abstract: Oral lichen planus (OLP) and burning mouth syndrome (BMS) are chronic oral conditions associated with persistent pain, but direct comparisons of their pain profiles and contributing factors remain limited. This study compared factors influencing pain perception between OLP and BMS. This cross-sectional study included 46 patients with OLP and 50 with BMS. Pain characteristics, pain catastrophizing, and quality of life were assessed using the Brief Pain Inventory-Korean version, Pain Catastrophizing Scale-Korean version, and a Korean-language Oral Potentially Malignant Disorders Quality of Life questionnaire. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test; Mann-Whitney U or independent t-tests were applied accordingly, and effect sizes were calculated using Cohen's d. Pain intensity predictors were identified using stepwise multiple linear regression. Patients with BMS reported higher pain intensity (p ≤ 0.003, d = -1.22 to -0.63) and catastrophizing (p = 0.005, d = -0.56) than those with OLP, whereas patients with OLP showed greater mastication-related pain interference (p = 0.002, d = 0.74) and poorer quality of life (p = 0.020, d = 0.50). Regression identified mastication and rumination in OLP (adjusted R2 = 0.419) and sleep disturbance, rumination, and magnification in BMS (adjusted R2 = 0.454) as primary predictors. Age stratification revealed an opposite age-pain relationship: older patients with BMS (>60 years) had higher pain intensity (p < 0.001), whereas younger patients with OLP (≤60 years) reported higher pain intensity (p = 0.037). Pain interference was more interconnected across life domains in OLP (27 correlations with |r| > 0.5) than in BMS (6 correlations). OLP and BMS exhibit distinct pain profiles, with OLP characterized by widespread functional interference influenced by mastication-related and cognitive factors, and BMS marked by higher pain intensity with prominent psychological contributors. Condition-specific strategies incorporating cognitive behavioral therapy targeting rumination may improve pain-related outcomes.
